questions.explanation:
Any change of state is a physical change
EXAMPLES OF CHEMICAL CHANGE
a. Burning of wood (or anything else)
b. Dissolution of active metal in cold water
$2Na + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + H_2$
c. Passing steam over red hot iron or coke
$Fe + 4H_2O \rightarrow Fe_3O_4 + 4H_2$
$C + H_2O \rightarrow CO + H_2$
d. Slaking of lime
$CaO + H_2O \rightarrow Ca(OH)_2$
e. Rusting of iron in moist air or aerated water
$4Fe + 2xH_2O + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2Fe_2O_3 x H_2O$
f. Heating Limestone
$CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2$
g. Passing a stream of hydrogen over heated copper (II) Oxide: $CuO + H_2 \rightarrow Cu + H_2O$
h. Adding water to calcium dicarbide:
$CaC_2 + H_2O \rightarrow CaO + C_2H_2$
i. Action of acid on metals, trioxocarbonates (IV) or alkalis (bases): $Zn + HCl \rightarrow ZnCl_2 + H_2$
$CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2$
$NaOH + HCl \rightarrow NaCl + H_2O$
j. Charring of sugar: $C_6H_{12}O_6 + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow 6C + 6H_2O$
k. Fermentation of starch to ethyl alcohol
l. redox changes in electrochemical/electrolytic cell

Mole ratio: C (100-14.29)/12 = 7.12 H 14.29/1 = 14.29. Dividing by the smallest (i.e 7.12) 1 : 2

Mass conc. = Molar conc. x Molar mass
Or 8 = 0.08M $\Rightarrow$ M = $\frac{8}{0.08} = 100gmol^{-1}$

Position of ions in the electrochemical series (a) Metallic ion lower in the series preferentially discharge ahead of the ones higher up e.g $Cu^{2+}$ instead of $H^+$, $Fe^{2+}$, $Mg^{2+}$ e.t.c. (b) Non-metallic ion higher in the series ahead of lower Ones e.g $OH^-$ instead of $Cl^-$ ii. Concentration of ion in solution: (a) A more concentrated ion ahead of the less concentrated irrespective of position in the series. e.g $Cl^-$ ahead of $OH^-$ if more concentrated as here. (b) If the gap between the two competing ion is wide, however, the effect of concentration is insignificant e.g $Cu^{2+}$ and $Na^+$ or $Cl^-$ and $F^-$ iii. Nature of Electrode used e.g Hg cathode discharges the powerful Na as Sodium amalgam (Na/Hg) while copper electrodes influence the activities at electrodes when $CuSO_4$ is the electrolyte (see Q7)

questions.explanation: At Anode - $Cl^-$ discharged instead of $OH^-$ since the former is more concentrated: $2Cl^- \rightarrow Cl_2 + 2e^-$ Thus effluent might be HCl: $H_2 + Cl_2 \rightarrow 2HCl$ NOTE: $H_2$ couldn't have been the ultimate effluent because hydrogen, on exposure to air, reacts with $O_2$ instantly and explosively: $2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O$ $4OH^- \rightarrow 2H_2O + O_2 + 4e^-$ $4Ag^+ + 4e^- \rightarrow 4Ag$ $4mol Ag \equiv 1mol of O_2$ $4(108g)Ag \equiv 22.4dm^3 O_2$ Then $10.8g Ag \equiv x dm^3 O_2$ Cross $x = \frac{22.4 \times 10.8}{4 \times 108} = 0.56dm^3$

questions.question: In recharging a lead-acid accumulator, the reaction at the cathode can be represented as
questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.explanation:
When a lead acid accumulator discharges: I. At Anode: $Pb \rightarrow Pb^{2+} + 2e^-$ (lead rod as anode) $2H_2SO_{4(aq)} \rightarrow 4H^+ + 2SO_4^{2-}$ (electrolyte)
$Pb^{2+} + SO_4^{2-} \rightarrow PbSO_{4(s)}$ (deposition) ii. At Cathode: $PbO_2 + 4H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb^{2+} + 2H_2O$ (cathode as $PbO_2$) $Pb^{2+} + SO_4^{2-} \rightarrow PbSO_4$ (deposition) When the accumulator recharges: Cathode (our former anode) $PbSO_4 \begin{cases} Pb^{2+} \rightarrow Pb \text{[can now be reused as anode]} \\ SO_4^{2-} \end{cases}$ Anode (our former cathode) $\xrightarrow{+H_2O} PbSO_4 \begin{cases} Pb^{2+} \\ SO_4^{2-} \end{cases} \rightarrow PbO_2 + 4H^+ + 2e$ [$PbO_2$ reused] NOTE: Cathode and anode in discharging cells are interchanged in recharging cells but oxidation at anode, and reduction at cathode remain valid.

questions.section: Chapter 16 Non-metals Hydrogen Oxygen Carbon Phosphorus

questions.explanation:
Continuing from Q1, a neutral oxide is neither acidic nor Basic e.g $H_2O$ / CO / $N_2O$ / NO
NOTE: Other oxides
i. Peroxides - They contain higher proportion of Oxygen than ordinarily contained in normal oxides.
e.g $H_2O_2$, $Na_2O_2$, $CaO_2$ and $BaO_2$ as opposed to $H_2O$, $Na_2O$, CaO and BaO respectively.
Peroxides produce hydrogen Peroxide ($H_2O_2$) with acids:
$Na_2O_2 + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow Na_2SO_4 + H_2O_2$
ii. Higher oxides - Resemble peroxides but would not produce hydrogen peroxides with acid as above
e.g $PbO_2$, $MnO_2$.
iii. Mixed Oxides - Another set of higher oxides containing two different oxides
A. Iron(II)diiron(III) oxide ($Fe_3O_4$)
$Fe_3O_4 = \underset{\text{Iron(II)oxide}}{FeO} + \underset{\text{Iron(III)oxide}}{Fe_2O_3}$
B. Dilead(II)lead(IV) oxide ($Pb_3O_4$)
$Pb_3O_4 = \underset{\text{Dilead(II)oxide}}{2PbO (or Pb_2O_2)} + \underset{\text{Lead(IV)oxide}}{PbO_2}$

NEXT TIME: Oxidation of $H_2S$ by $HNO_3$: $2HNO_3 + H_2S \rightarrow 2H_2O + 2NO_2 + S$ [Using dilute $HNO_3$] $8HNO_3 + H_2S \rightarrow 4H_2O + 8NO_2 + H_2SO_4$ [Conc. $HNO_3$]

questions.explanation: Oxidation of a secondary Alkanol yields an Alkanone CLASSIFICATION OF ALKANOLS 1. Primary alkanol - One alkyl group attached to the C atom which carries the functional group: [diagrams of R-CH2-OH e.g. propan-1-ol] 2. Secondary alkanol - has two alkyl groups so attached: [diagrams e.g. propan-2-ol] 3. Tertiary alkanol - has three alkyl groups [diagrams e.g. 2-methylbutan-2-ol] KEY: The Alkyl(s) attached is/are asterisked in the examples. NOTE: 1. For other method of classifying alkanols see Q5 2. $1^{\circ}$ alkanol oxidized to alkanal then to alkanoic acid; $2^{\circ}$ alkanol oxidized to alkanone but not any further; $3^{\circ}$ alkanol not (easily) oxidized. 3. To identify $1^{\circ}$, $2^{\circ}$ and $3^{\circ}$ Alkanols at a glance i.e from their names and without necessarily writing out their structural formulae, just follow this guide: *PRIMARY ALKANOLS 1. Alkan-x-ol where x = 1 e.g. butan-1-ol 2. y-Alkylalkan-x-ol where x = 1, just ignore y e.g. 3-methylbutan-1ol *SECONDARY ALKANOLS 1. Alkan-x-ol when $x \ge 2$ e.g. butan-2-ol/butan-3-ol 2. y-alkylalkan-x-ol $x \ge 2$ and $x \ne y$ e.g. 3-methylbutan-2-ol [2 and 3 are not equal] *TERTIARY ALKANOLS Always as: y-alkylalkan-x-ol where $x \ge 2$ and x = y e.g. 2-methylbutan-2-ol *Teachers are implored to thoroughly explain these to their students.

questions.question: Alkanals can be differentiated from alkanones by reaction with
questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.explanation: Tollen's reagent is a mild oxidizing agent which can oxidize only the alkanals (as mild reducing agents) but not the even milder reducing agents, the alkanones NOTE: i. The mirror-like deposit of silver is a positive test for Alkanals. ii. These related but distinct families of organic compounds can also be differentiated using another mild oxidizing agent called Fehling's solution which contains copper (II) ion complexes. iii. Formation of brick–red coloration with Fehling's solution is also positive for alkanals [Cu$^{2+}$] + Alkanal $\rightarrow$ [Cu$^{+}$] brick-red iv. Alkanals (or aldehydes) and alkanones (or ketones) are related because they both have carbonyl group (see Q138) v. Tollen's and Fehling's are also used to test for reducing sugars base on the same principle above

questions.question: An example of a polysaccharide is
questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.explanation: A complex Sugar NOTE: 1. Monosaccharides (also called simple sugars) are sweet and water soluble e.g glucose, fructose, galactose, mannose; they are isomers and Hexoses (C$_{6}$H$_{12}$O$_{6}$) 2. Disaccharides (or double sugars) are sweet, water soluble and are condensation products of two monosaccharide units and they include: Maltose = Glucose + Glucose Sucrose = Glucose + Fructose Lactose = Glucose + Galactose C$_{6}$H$_{12}$O$_{6}$ + C$_{6}$H$_{12}$O$_{6}$ $\rightarrow$ C$_{12}$H$_{22}$O$_{11}$ + H$_{2}$O 3. Double sugars are isomeric C$_{12}$H$_{22}$O$_{11}$ 4. Polysaccharides (or complex sugars) are tasteless, insoluble carbohydrates containing long chains of repeated monosaccharide units after condensation e.g starch, cellulose, glycogen (animal starch) and inulin 5. Glucose $\Rightarrow$ Dextrose $\Rightarrow$ Grape sugar $\Rightarrow$ Blood sugar 6. Fructose $\Rightarrow$ Laevulose $\Rightarrow$ fruit sugar 7. Maltose $\Rightarrow$ Malt sugar 8. Sucrose $\Rightarrow$ cane sugar; 9. Lactose $\Rightarrow$ Milk sugar 10. Monosaccharides $\xrightarrow[Hydrolysis]{Condensation}$ Disaccharide

Conditions for optical activity i. Existence of a carbon atom (called chiral carbon) in a molecule of the compound and to which are attached four different substituent groups. ii. The compound and its isomer must be mirror images of each other and must not be superimposable on each other [Diagrams of lactic acid enantiomers about a Mirror: $CH_3$-$C^*$(H)(OH)-COOH and mirror image COOH-$C^*$(H)($CH_3$)-OH] *$C^*$= chiral carbon to which $CH_3$, H, OH and COOH are attached Lactic acid = 2-hydroxypropanoic acid. 3. In functional isomerism, isomers belong to different homologous series (hence have different functional groups) e.g propanal and propanone; ethanol and dimethyl ether etc
